findings.title: Uncaught std::stoi exception crashes the whole compiler on large integer literals
findings.description: build_number_token() calls std::stoi(build_string) with no try/catch. For any integer literal that exceeds INT_MAX (e.g. a 40-digit number), stoi throws std::out_of_range, which is never caught anywhere in scanner.cpp/parser.cpp/main.cpp, so the process aborts (SIGABRT). Reproduced directly with a standalone harness linking scanner.cpp: a source file containing only '99999999999999999999999999999999999999999' crashes with 'terminate called after throwing an instance of std::out_of_range; what(): stoi' (exit 134). std::stof at line 402 has the same unguarded-exception exposure for out-of-range floats.
findings.evidence: token_int_value = std::stoi(build_string); (scanner.cpp:410) — no surrounding try/catch in build_number_token or its callers.

findings.title: comment_handler() runs unconditionally inside // comments, letting a stray /* inside a line comment start real block-comment suppression
findings.description: The main Get_token() loop (lines 149-217) dispatches every character through what_is_char()/build_char_token() even while is_slash_comment is already true — it only uses is_slash_comment to discard the resulting tokens, it never skips the char classification itself. build_char_token()'s cases for '/' and '*' (lines 253-264, 311-321) unconditionally call comment_handler(), which has no guard for 'we are already inside a // comment'. So if a '//' comment's text happens to contain '/*', comment_handler() sets is_nested_commented=true for real, and that state persists past the end of the line (end_line_handler() only resets is_slash_comment, not is_nested_commented). Verified directly: the source '// this is a comment /* not really a block start\nx\n' produces zero real tokens and goes straight to T_INVALID at EOF with is_nested_commented still 1 — the identifier 'x' on the next line is silently swallowed.
findings.evidence: Harness output for '// ... /* not really a block start\nx': '0: type=283 (INVALID) line=0 ... is_nested_commented=1 nested_counter=1' — no IDENTIFIER token for x was ever produced.

findings.title: nested_comment_counter can be driven negative by a stray '*/' and never resets, causing later legitimate nested comments to close one level early and leak commented-out code as real tokens
findings.description: In comment_handler(), the close branch does 'nested_comment_counter--;' with no floor check and no verification that a nested comment was actually open. A stray '*/' anywhere in the file (including one leaked from inside a '//' comment per the previous finding, or simply mistyped in code) decrements the counter below zero and it never self-corrects (there is no reset to 0 on file boundaries or on detecting an already-non-open state). Because the open branch (line 552, 'nested_comment_counter++') and close branch use '<= 0' rather than tracking a true open/closed boolean stack, a counter starting at -1 causes a subsequently well-formed two-level nested comment '/* level1 /* level2 */ ... */' to have is_nested_commented flip to false after only the FIRST closing '*/', exposing the remainder of the outer comment's body as real source tokens. Verified: with a preceding '// oops */ stray close' line, the input '/* level1 /* level2 */ leaked_identifier_should_be_hidden */\nz' produced the token stream IDENTIFIER('leaked_identifier_should_be_hidden'), IDENTIFIER('z') — the text that should have stayed hidden inside the outer comment leaked out as a real identifier token. A control run without the preceding stray '*/' correctly hides it (only 'z' is emitted).
findings.evidence: Harness output difference: with corrupting stray '*/' -> '0: type=278 (IDENTIFIER) ... str=[leaked_identifier_should_be_hidden] ... nested_counter=0' then '1: type=278 (IDENTIFIER) ... str=[z]'; control (no stray '*/') -> only '0: type=278 (IDENTIFIER) ... str=[z]'.

findings.title: Number literal with a second decimal point silently discards the already-scanned digits with no reported error
findings.description: build_number_token()'s multi-decimal check sets error_detected=true and does a bare 'return;' (line 373-374) without ever setting Current_token->type/floatValue/intValue/line_found. The characters already appended to build_string (e.g. the '1.2' prefix of '1.2.3') are simply thrown away — no token is ever produced for that data, and no error message reaches the user (error_detected is never read anywhere, see separate finding). Verified: scanning '12 1.2 1.2.3 100' yields tokens INTEGER(12), FLOAT(1.2), PERIOD, INTEGER(3) — i.e. the '1.2' portion of the third literal vanished entirely and the second '.' was reinterpreted as an unrelated PERIOD token.
findings.evidence: Harness output for '12 1.2 1.2.3 100': '2: type=46 (PERIOD) ... char=[.]' followed by '3: type=279 (INTEGER_VALUE) ... int=3' — no token at all represents the discarded '1.2' prefix of the third literal.

findings.title: Numeric literal underscore digit-group separators from the grammar are not tokenized as part of the number
findings.description: The spec grammar is <number> ::= [0-9][0-9_]*[.[0-9_]*] (spec2023.txt line 98), i.e. underscores are legal digit-group separators both before and after the decimal point. build_number_token()'s consumption loop only tests 'isdigit(next_char) || next_char == '.'' — underscore is not accepted, so '1_000' or '3.1_4' are not scanned as single number tokens. Verified: '1_000\n' produces INTEGER(1), UNDERSCORE, INTEGER(0) (three tokens, and the numeric value is wrong — '000' parses to 0, not 1000), and '3.1_4\n' produces FLOAT(3.1), UNDERSCORE, INTEGER(4).
findings.evidence: spec2023.txt:98 '<number> ::= [0-9][0-9_]*[.[0-9_]*]'; scanner.cpp:363 'while (isdigit(next_char) || next_char == '.')' has no '_' case. Harness output for '1_000': '0: ...INTEGER_VALUE... int=1', '1: ...UNDERSCORE...', '2: ...INTEGER_VALUE... int=0'.

findings.title: scanner::error_detected is write-only across the entire codebase — illegal characters are never reported as errors, contrary to the spec
findings.description: The project spec requires: 'Illegal characters should be treated as white-space separators and reported as errors.' invalid_char_test()'s else branch (the only code path that flags a truly illegal/unrecognized character) only sets scanner::error_detected=true and otherwise silently skips the character. A repo-wide grep confirms error_detected is declared in scanner.h:114, assigned in scanner.cpp at lines 373, 489, 520, and never read anywhere else in the codebase (not in parser.cpp, parser.h, main.cpp, or Typechecker.cpp) — unlike the analogous is_nested_commented/quote_status flags, which the parser does check (parser.cpp:74,99,2444) to report unterminated-comment/unterminated-string errors. So illegal characters are correctly skipped as whitespace but the 'reported as errors' half of the requirement is unimplemented.
findings.evidence: grep -rn "error_detected" across the repo only shows scanner.h:114 (declaration) and scanner.cpp:373,489,520 (assignments) — no reads anywhere else, versus is_nested_commented/quote_status which parser.cpp does read for error reporting.

findings.title: error_detected is spuriously true from the very first call regardless of actual input, due to the char=0 priming character being run through invalid_char_test()
findings.description: current_char and next_char default-initialize to 0 (scanner.h:100,102). On the very first iteration of Get_token()'s while(true) loop, current_char is set to this 0 and dispatched through what_is_char(0) -> invalid_char_test(), whose else branch (current_char is neither '\n' nor isspace) sets error_detected=true unconditionally on every run, before a single real character of the file has been examined. Verified: even scanning a fully well-formed file like 'a := 5;' shows error_detected=1 from the very first emitted token onward. This means even if error_detected were wired up for reporting (see previous finding), it would be useless as it's always true.
findings.evidence: scanner.h:100 'char next_char = 0;', scanner.h:102 'char current_char = 0;'; harness run on 'a := 5;\n' (no illegal characters) shows 'error_detected=1' on token 0 already.

findings.title: Scanner never tokenizes compound operators (:=, ==, !=, <=, >=); whitespace-separated single characters are indistinguishable from adjacent ones
findings.description: Unlike comment_handler(), which does source.peek()-based lookahead to combine '/' + '/' or '/' + '*' into comment tokens, build_char_token()'s cases for ':' , '=', '<', '>', '!' (lines 335-345, 248-250, 306-308, 302-304, 331-333) do no lookahead at all — each becomes its own single-character token, and the parser reconstructs ':=' / '==' / '!=' / '<=' / '>=' from two consecutive raw tokens (parser.cpp Get_Valid_Token / parse_relation). Because the scanner discards whitespace without recording any adjacency/column information (token.column_found is also never populated — see separate finding), two non-adjacent occurrences of the same character (e.g. 'x = = y' or 'x : = 5;') produce exactly the same token sequence as the real compound operator and get silently accepted downstream as '==' / ':='. Verified: 'x = = y\n' yields IDENTIFIER, ASSIGN, ASSIGN, IDENTIFIER — identical in shape to what 'x == y' would produce; likewise 'x : = 5;' yields COLON then ASSIGN just like ':='.
findings.evidence: Harness output for 'x = = y': tokens 1 and 2 are both 'type=61 (ASSIGN(=))' with a literal space between the two '=' characters in the source, with no distinguishing information in either token.

findings.title: token::identifier_data_type has no default member initializer, unlike every sibling field
findings.description: Every other data field in class token has an explicit default (type=0, line_found=0, column_found=0, global_scope=false, scope_id=0, intValue=0, stringValue="", boolValue=false, floatValue=0.0, charValue=0, first_token_on_line=false, identifer_type=I_NONE, is_array=false), but 'data_types identifier_data_type;' (line 126) is left with no initializer. Since token has no user-declared default constructor (the one sketched at lines 87-89 is commented out), every 'new token' / local 'token x;' (used pervasively in scanner.cpp, e.g. Current_token = new token at scanner.cpp:120,147,201,207, and in SymbolTable.cpp's insert_stringValue) leaves identifier_data_type holding indeterminate memory. This is exactly the kind of uninitialized-field pattern that would produce a garbage data_types value read later by the type checker/symbol table for any token whose data type was never explicitly assigned, and because token's destructor (token.h:92-106) resets fields to known values only on destruction (not construction), the stale value persists for the whole lifetime of a freshly-built token until something explicitly assigns identifier_data_type.
findings.evidence: token.h:122 'identifier_types identifer_type = I_NONE;' has a default, but token.h:126 'data_types identifier_data_type;' does not — no '= TYPE_NONE'.

findings.title: STRING_VALUE token's line_found reflects the closing line (or EOF) rather than the string's starting line
findings.description: string_value_builder() saves the opening line in quote_opener (line 497, used only by the parser for the 'quotation left open' error), but sets the returned token's own line_found using current_line AFTER the character-consuming loop (line 531) — i.e. the line where the closing quote (or EOF) was reached, which is incremented during the loop for every embedded newline (lines 510-515). For a string literal that spans multiple physical lines (the grammar's "[^"]*" does not exclude newline, and the scanner does not reject embedded newlines), the token handed to the parser/typechecker for later error messages carries the wrong line number. Verified with an unterminated multi-line string: a string opened on line 1 that runs to EOF on line 4 is reported with line_found=4.
findings.evidence: Harness output for a string starting on source line 1 and running (unterminated) through line 4: '3: type=281 (STRING_VALUE) line=4 ...'.

findings.title: token::column_found is declared but never assigned anywhere in the scanner
findings.description: column_found (declared at token.h:109, defaulted to 0) is never written to by any function in scanner.cpp — a repo-wide grep for 'column_found'/'column' outside token.h finds no assignment site. Every token therefore reports column 0 regardless of its actual source position, so this half-implemented feature provides no positional precision beyond the line number, and (combined with the missing operator-adjacency tracking noted separately) leaves the scanner with no way to detect that two tokens were separated by whitespace.
findings.evidence: grep -n "column_found|column" across scanner.cpp/scanner.h/token.h only shows the token.h declaration and destructor reset — no scanner.cpp assignment.

findings.title: boolValue is never populated for T_TRUE/T_FALSE reserved-word tokens
findings.description: SymbolTable::insert_stringValue() (used to seed 'true'->T_TRUE and 'false'->T_FALSE in init_reserved_words) only sets new_token->type and new_token->stringValue; boolValue is left at its default (false). build_string_token() in scanner.cpp then simply copies this seeded token via '*Current_token = symbol_table.map[build_string];' (scanner.cpp:444/451), so a scanned 'true' literal ends up with token.type==T_TRUE but token.boolValue==false, and a 'false' literal is likewise indistinguishable from 'true' by boolValue alone. Currently the parser/typechecker appear to branch on token.type (T_TRUE vs T_FALSE) rather than reading boolValue for these tokens (parser.cpp:2462-2481), so the immediate observable impact is limited today, but the field is silently wrong for any future consumer that trusts token.boolValue for a boolean literal.
findings.evidence: SymbolTable.cpp:42-43 'new_token->type = type_of_token; new_token->stringValue = stringValue;' — no boolValue assignment; SymbolTable.cpp:12-32 seeds 'true'/'false' via this function.

findings.title: ctype.h classification functions are called with a plain (signed) char argument without an unsigned char cast
findings.description: what_is_char() calls isalpha(test_char)/isdigit(test_char) (lines 33,37) and invalid_char_test() calls isspace(current_char) (line 475), and build_number_token()/build_string_token() call isdigit/isalpha on next_char (lines 363, 422) — all with a bare 'char', which is signed on the target platform (x86-64 Linux/g++). Per the C standard, these functions require an argument representable as unsigned char or EOF; passing a negative char value (e.g. any raw byte >=0x80, such as would appear in a UTF-8-encoded source file or stray binary content) is undefined behavior. On this glibc build a quick test with 0xFF/0xFE bytes in a source file did not crash (glibc's ctype table tolerates the negative range in practice), so the practical impact observed here was limited to those bytes being classified as 'invalid_char' and skipped, but the code relies on non-portable, standard-violating behavior.
findings.evidence: scanner.cpp:33 'if (isalpha(test_char))' and :37 'else if (isdigit(test_char))' where test_char is declared 'char' (scanner.h:64 'int what_is_char(char test_char);'); harness test with bytes 0xFF 0xFE embedded in source did not crash but relies on glibc-specific tolerance rather than defined behavior.

findings.title: T_INVALID/EOF token reports line_found=0 when EOF is reached before any real token was ever returned
findings.description: Get_token()'s EOF branch does '*Current_token = last_sent_token; Current_token->type = T_INVALID;' (lines 156-158). If the file never produces a real token before EOF (e.g. a file consisting solely of an unterminated block comment), last_sent_token is still the default-constructed token from scanner.h:140 (line_found=0), so the T_INVALID token returned to the parser reports line 0 instead of a line near the actual end of file, which would produce a misleading location in any downstream 'unexpected EOF' style error message.
findings.evidence: Harness output for a file consisting only of '/* start of comment\nx := 5;\n' (unterminated comment, no valid token ever emitted): '0: type=283 (INVALID) line=0 ... is_nested_commented=1 nested_counter=1'.

notes:
Scope covered: scanner.cpp, scanner.h, token.h, and SymbolTable.cpp/.h reserved-word/char seeding (SymbolTable.cpp init_reserved_words/init_reserved_chars, Tolower_string in CustomFunctions.cpp). I built a standalone test harness (scanner.cpp + SymbolTable.cpp + CustomFunctions.cpp + ScopeTable.cpp, no parser needed) at /tmp/claude-1000/-datadrive-data-compiler-course/e0905122-5395-4b36-add9-f6a81e41bd28/scratchpad/scantest/harness.cpp and used it to empirically confirm every finding marked speculative:false against crafted .src inputs (also in that directory) — these are not repo files and were not committed; no repo files were modified.

Things verified as CORRECT (not bugs), for context: case-insensitive identifier/reserved-word folding to lowercase (spec item 2) works correctly (BEGIN/begin/Begin all normalize to the same T_BEGIN token); whitespace/tab/newline skipping and line counting work correctly for the normal (non-pathological) cases; well-formed non-corrupted nested block comments correctly hide their contents (control test); the unterminated-string and unterminated-block-comment cases ARE eventually reported by the parser via Lexer->quote_status/quote_opener and Lexer->is_nested_commented/nested_comment_line (parser.cpp:74,99,2444-2447) — so those two specific failure modes are NOT unreported, only the generic 'illegal character' and 'multiple decimal points' failure modes are unreported (both funnel solely through the dead scanner::error_detected flag).

Root-cause investigation for the parser's 'random junk' defensive loop (parser.cpp:52, 'while (Next_parse_token_type > T_INVALID || Next_parse_token_type < 0)'): I could not find a currently-reachable scanner code path that produces a token.type outside [0, T_INVALID=283] — all char tokens use named ASCII-range enum constants, all reserved words/identifiers come from the seeded/inserted symbol_table map (always valid enum values), and the one path that leaves Current_token->type at its default 0 (build_number_token's multi-decimal-error early return) is filtered out INSIDE Get_token()'s own retry loop (the `type != 0` check) and never actually returned to the parser — confirmed by testing '1.2.3' end-to-end through the scanner: no type=0 token is ever emitted externally, the loop just silently discards that partial number and resumes on the next character. So the specific 'garbage token type >283 or <0' scenario the parser comment complains about was not reproducible from the current scanner.cpp/token.h source by static analysis or by direct harness testing; the closest concrete 'uninitialized field' defect I could confirm by inspection is token::identifier_data_type lacking a default initializer (token.h:126), which is a different field from the one the parser's junk-filter checks (token.type), so I flagged it separately and marked the ctype-UB and boolValue findings as speculative on downstream impact since I could not exercise the parser/typechecker to observe consequences from this scanner-only harness.

CLAUDE.md was skimmed only to avoid duplicating its listed known bug (Typechecker::second_relation_token_chains missing return, unrelated to the scanner); none of the findings above overlap with anything mentioned there. All line numbers cited were confirmed by direct reads of the current repo files (not from memory).
